extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patent attorneys, and patent examiners dealing with German national patent procedures (German Patent and Trade Mark Office)
extracted.subtask_description: Explanatory and procedural guidelines for preparing, examining, and deciding patent applications in Germany, including special rules for biotechnological and computer-implemented inventions and deposit requirements for biological material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description must indicate the invention and avoid unnecessary information
rubrics_metrics.description: The invention for which patent protection is sought in the patent claims must be indicated in the description; the description must not contain any information that is obviously not necessary for explaining the invention (section 34 (3) number 4 Patent Act and section 10 Patent Ordinance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The description and drawings are used to interpret the claims (section 14 Patent Act). If agreement on claim wording is reached, the applicant must align the description with the valid claims and comply with Patent Ordinance requirements. To simplify, literal quotation of claim parts in the description may be replaced by references to those claim parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant must indicate relevant state of the art in the description when requested
rubrics_metrics.description: At the request of the German Patent and Trade Mark Office, the applicant must indicate the (relevant) state of the art known to him and include it in the description (section 7 Patent Act; section 10 (2) number 2 Patent Ordinance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentioning relevant prior art does not require the applicant to evaluate or assess it. Disparaging remarks on the state of the art must be omitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title must indicate the invention and consider subsidiary claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The title of the invention, which must be indicated at the beginning of the description (section 10 (1) in conjunction with section 4 (2) number 2 of the Patent Ordinance), should take into account all subsidiary patent claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copies of certain documents are provided only upon application and in paper form
rubrics_metrics.description: Copies are made only upon application of one of the persons concerned and only in paper form (section 47 (1) sentence 2 Patent Act).

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure and content of decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions contain a caption (parties and representatives), an operative part (tenor) separated from the reasons, and a statement of reasons consisting of facts of the case and the reasons for the decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Facts should briefly describe essential content of claims and means of attack/defence, emphasizing motions submitted. Reasons should summarise the factual and legal considerations underpinning the decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasons must cover all points relevant to the decision and state detailed considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: The reasons must cover all points at issue relevant to the decision and state in detail all considerations on questions of fact and law which made the examining section reach its decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotation of unpublished decisions should be avoided where possible, though the examining section may adopt views from unpublished decisions and their reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: When reasons may be abbreviated or omitted
rubrics_metrics.description: Reasons need not be given in detail if the application is refused because deficiencies expressly notified have not been removed and the applicant has not commented; in such cases reference may be made to the communication's reasons. Reasons need not be given if the applicant is the only party and his request has been allowed (section 47 (1) sentence 4 Patent Act).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: decision to grant as requested or allowing reinstatement in single‑party procedures. If reinstatement is allowed, grounds should be recorded in a short file note.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written decision must include instructions about right to appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: The written execution of a decision must be accompanied by instructions concerning the right to appeal (section 47 (2) sentence 1 Patent Act).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omitted or incorrect instructions can extend the appeal period (appeal may still be filed within one year of service), so instructions must be rectified if incorrect; otherwise appeals may become admissible indefinitely in some cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectiveness of decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions take effect when delivered or formally served. For in‑office purposes a self‑obligation arises already upon handing the decision to the document dispatching service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision to grant patent — statutory criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: The examining section decides to grant the patent if the subject matter is patentable pursuant to sections 1 to 5 Patent Act, the application complies with sections 34, 37 and 38 Patent Act, and any remedyable deficiencies (e.g., in the abstract under section 45 (1)) have been remedied (section 49 Patent Act).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision to grant cannot be revoked even if contrary to law. Grant is published in the Patent Gazette and statutory effects arise with publication (section 58 Patent Act).

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision to refuse application — statutory criteria and procedural safeguard
rubrics_metrics.description: The examining section refuses the application if the invention is not patentable under sections 1 to 5 Patent Act or if deficiencies objected to under section 45 (1) were not remedied (section 48 Patent Act).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a general rule, a refusal may only be based on circumstances previously communicated to the applicant to give opportunity to comment (section 48 sentence 2 in conjunction with section 42 (3) sentence 2 Patent Act).

rubrics_metrics.name: Right and timing of appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions of the examining sections that contain a final regulation with external effect are subject to appeal (section 73 (1) Patent Act). The appeal must be filed in writing with the DPMA within one month after service (section 73 (2) sentence 1 Patent Act).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An appeal fee under the Patent Costs Act is due upon filing; if not paid within the appeal period, the appeal is deemed not filed (Patent Costs Act in conjunction with section 73 (2)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination of appeal by examining section
rubrics_metrics.description: The examining section must first examine whether a received appeal is admissible and second whether it is well‑founded; whether the decision is rectified depends on this examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the appeal is well‑founded the examining section may rectify its decision (section 73 (3) sentence 1). Rectification may be opposed by another party to the proceedings; rectification is only possible if the appeal is admissible (filed in due time and form) and the grounds for refusal no longer exist (e.g., applicant's submissions convinced the section or requested modifications were made).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reimbursement of appeal fee
rubrics_metrics.description: Reimbursement of the appeal fee must be ordered if it would be inequitable to retain the fee (section 73 (3) sentence 2 Patent Act).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: obvious error by the German Patent and Trade Mark Office forcing the appellant to appeal, or unsuitable handling of the procedure that made the appeal necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of timely submissions after appeal filing
rubrics_metrics.description: If reasons and/or new documents are submitted within one month from filing the appeal and an examination reveals the appeal is well‑founded, the decision must be rectified; otherwise the appeal must be forwarded to the Federal Patent Court without comment on its merits (section 73 (3) sentence 3 Patent Act).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of biotechnological inventions (subject matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Biotechnological inventions are those whose subject matter is a product consisting of or containing biological material or a process by which biological material is produced, processed or used. Biological material contains genetic information (its structural design) and is capable of reproducing itself or being reproduced in a biological system; a microbiological process involves or results in microbiological material (section 2a (3) Patent Act).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such inventions are eligible for protection under the Patent Act and Directive 98/44/EC; statutory transposition and later amendments (e.g., exclusions for plants and animals produced exclusively by essentially biological processes) must be observed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of deposit of biological material
rubrics_metrics.description: The purpose of depositing biological material is to supplement disclosure where the biological material cannot be described in a manner enabling reproduction by a person skilled in the art (section 1 (1) Ordinance on the Deposit of Biological Material).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The deposit must ensure the disclosure required by section 34 (4) Patent Act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deposit can substitute for description for microbiological products but not always for processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Microbiological processes and products can be protected by patent even if a sample of the biological material is deposited instead of a descriptive manufacturing process. However, if the application concerns the microbiological process itself, deposit of the product does not replace proof of reproducibility of the process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vectors (e.g., plasmids) need not be deposited if a reproducible manufacturing process or a complete nucleotide sequence is indicated. Complete nucleotide sequences must be submitted electronically (section 11 Patent Ordinance and Annex 1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Options for recognised depositary and implications (Budapest Treaty vs national institutions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A due deposit may be made at an international depositary authority under the Budapest Treaty or at recognised scientific institutions that guarantee storage and furnishing of samples and independence from applicant/depositor (sections 2 and 8 Ordinance on the Deposit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Difference: for Budapest Treaty deposits no specific declaration authorising furnishing of samples is required for third‑party furnishing; for non‑Budapest deposits a declaration is governed by section 4 of the Ordinance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Date of deposit requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Biological material must be deposited with a recognised depositary institution not later than the date of filing or the priority date (section 1 (1) Ordinance on the Deposit).

rubrics_metrics.name: Information on deposit required in application and allowable late filing of deposit file number
rubrics_metrics.description: The application as originally filed must contain relevant information on properties of the deposited material known to the applicant, the depositary institution and the deposit file number (section 1 (1) numbers 2 and 3 Ordinance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a third party already deposited the material, no further deposit is required provided first deposit ensures clear and sufficient disclosure. The deposit file number may be filed subsequently within 16 months after filing or priority date (section 3 (1) Ordinance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration of storage obligations for deposited biological material
rubrics_metrics.description: Deposited biological material must be stored for five years from receipt of the last request for furnishing, but at least five years longer than the legally stipulated maximum term of protection of all industrial property rights referring to the deposited material (section 7 Ordinance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For Budapest Treaty deposits a minimum storage period of 30 years from deposit applies (Rule 9.1 Budapest Treaty).

rubrics_metrics.name: Irrevocable declaration authorising furnishing of samples
rubrics_metrics.description: The applicant must make the deposited biological material available to the depositary from the date of filing by making an irrevocable declaration authorising the furnishing of samples without reservation (section 4 (1) Ordinance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Furnishing of samples is governed by section 5 Ordinance; before first publication samples are limited in availability; after first publication samples are made available to any person on request (subject to depositor's restrictions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Access to samples before and after publication and possible restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Until first publication a sample is made available only to the depositor or the DPMA and in special cases to the applicant/third party by decision or depositor's consent. From first publication to grant, biological material is made available to any person on request (section 5 Ordinance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The depositor may restrict access by furnishing a sample only to an independent expert appointed by requester (expert solution). After grant (or grant of SPC), samples are available to anyone notwithstanding later invalidity. If application is refused/withdrawn, access may (on applicant request) be limited to independent expert for 20 years from filing (section 5 (2)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Form, undertakings and expert handling for furnishing samples
rubrics_metrics.description: Requests for access must be submitted using the prescribed form (section 5 (5) Ordinance). A sample is furnished only if the requester undertakes not to make material available to third parties and not to use it except for testing (undertaking; section 6 (1) Ordinance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant/proprietor (and depositor in third‑party deposits) may waive the undertaking limited to testing. If furnished to an independent expert, the expert must submit the undertaking (section 6 (2)). For Budapest Treaty deposits no separate declaration is required but applicant may still restrict furnishing (Rule 11.2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of deposit must be provided or deficiency objected to
rubrics_metrics.description: If required proof of deposit is not attached to the application, the deficiency (if obvious) must be objected to within the examination of obvious deficiencies; otherwise during the examination procedure the applicant must be invited to present appropriate proof (certificate of deposit or declaration authorising furnishing, if required).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and scope of programme‑related (computer‑implemented) inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Programme-related inventions are inventions whose implementation involves the use of a computer, network or other programmable apparatus and which have at least one feature realised wholly or partly by a computer program (computer‑implemented inventions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They relate to devices and processes (programs) of electronic data processing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technicity requirement for computer‑implemented inventions (section 1(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents are granted only for inventions that are new, involve an inventive step, are industrially applicable (sections 1(1) Patent Act) and have technical character. Technical character generally exists if the invention contains teachings for achieving a result following clear causal steps by controlling natural forces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is not necessary that the causal result be obtained by direct application of controllable natural forces without human intellectual power as an intermediate step; technical character can arise from knowledge based on technical considerations and its realisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program‑related inventions considered technical if serving a technical device
rubrics_metrics.description: A program-related invention is considered to have technicity if the subject matter serves to process, store and transmit data by a technical device.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions to patentability (section 1(3),(4)) and how they apply
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain subject matter is not regarded as an invention as such: (a) discoveries, scientific theories and mathematical methods; (b) aesthetic creations; (c) schemes, rules and methods for mental acts, playing games or doing business and computer programs; (d) presentations of information (section 1 (3) Patent Act). Section 1 (4) clarifies that exclusion is for these activities 'as such'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program‑related inventions and combinations of excluded subject matter are as a rule eligible for patent protection because exclusion applies to the non‑technical subject matter as such. The exception is generally applied to processes but not to apparatus (Federal Court of Justice case law).

rubrics_metrics.name: Three‑stage examination approach for program‑related inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: A three‑stage approach: (1) clarify whether the subject matter has technical character (section 1 (1)); (2) examine whether the invention is excluded from patentability under the exceptions (section 1 (3) and (4)) using a unitary criterion; (3) assess novelty and inventive step such that only instructions that determine or influence the solution to a specific technical problem by technical means are taken into account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preliminary first two stages are normally based on the patent application alone and typically without considering state of the art (a rough filter). Even where an exception appears to exist, a search for prior art and full assessment should regularly be conducted. The examination sequence is not absolutely mandatory.
